commits.message:
fix(pretty): bound what print formats, and stop one number meaning two things

UNVERIFIED: tsc --noEmit passes; the vitest run was cut off by a context limit before completing. Run 'npm run lint && npm test' first.

Round-2 review findings. print now formats arbitrary data, reaching two Pretty behaviours previously only reachable deliberately: a large container expands one line per element (print(buffer) costs a line per byte), and nesting recurses uncapped. print now passes PRINT_DATA_BOUNDS (maxLength 100, maxDepth 16). Bounds belong to the convenience path, which formats whatever it is handed; a caller who built a Pretty has seen their data and still gets no defaults. Both bounds announce themselves ('... +N', '{...}'), so truncation is visible. maxDepth is new on PrettyOptions, unbounded by default. Map and Set gained the '... +N' marker arrays and objects already had.

The cap did not work when first written, and that is the substantive change. _format's 'depth' carried two meanings: output indentation, and depth in the data. The compact probe passes depth 0 (correct for layout, since a single-line form has no indentation), so 'depth >= maxDepth' never fired down the probe path and a 400-deep object still hung. They are now separate fields on a Frame: 'inset' resets, 'level' only increases. [LAW:types-are-the-program]

Also replaces the console-highlighter test, which the reviewer correctly showed proved nothing: ReprHighlighter styles the number in { a: 1 } too, so it passed whether or not forwarding worked. It now records what the console's highlighter was handed.

KNOWN, NOT FIXED, NOT FILED: Pretty._formatObject formats every child twice (compact probe, then expanded), so cost is exponential in nesting depth. Measured on pre-existing code: depth 10=1ms, 20=17ms, 24=166ms, ~30=seconds. Pre-existing and still reachable via new Pretty(deep); print is now bounded by maxDepth 16 so the hazard is closed on the path this PR opened. Real fix: compute each child's single-line form once. Wants its own ticket and review.

fix(pretty): carry the caller's highlighter, and survive the data it is handed

Routing `print`'s data arguments through `Pretty` handed three things to a
formatter that was only ever reached deliberately before, and it was not ready
for any of them.

`highlight` and a custom `highlighter` are console-wide settings and stopped
reaching data arguments: `Pretty` held a module-level `ReprHighlighter` and used
it unconditionally, so `print(42, { highlight: false })` stayed coloured and a
`Console` built with a custom highlighter silently lost it for every non-string
value. `PrettyOptions` now takes `highlighter`, defaulting to the same
`ReprHighlighter` so a standalone `new Pretty(x)` is unchanged, and `print`
passes the console's — or `NullHighlighter`, so the disabled case is an identity
operation rather than a skipped call.

Self-referential data crashed the caller. `_format` recursed forever and threw
`RangeError`, where the `String()` it replaced merely returned an unhelpful
line. The traversal now carries the objects open between the root and the
current node, joined on the way down and left on the way back up, and prints
`[Circular]` on re-entry. The leave-on-exit is the whole design: a set that only
grew would call a shared child — one object reached twice through sibling
paths — circular the second time, and both cases are tested because neither
pins that alone.

Typed arrays lost their structure. `Int8Array` carries a `toString` distinct
from `Object.prototype`'s, so the self-description arm claimed it and answered a
bare `1,2,3` — no brackets, nothing for the highlighter to colour per element,
and indistinguishable from the string. They now reach the arm that formats
sequences, above self-description for the same reason `Array` sits there.

Also drops the `[LAW:parse-dont-validate]` citation on `describesItself`. The
token is canonical, but the citation was inapt: that law is about a check
returning a type that could not have existed before it ran, and `describesItself`
returns a boolean — the validator shape the law contrasts against.

fix(console): let print say what a value is, instead of nothing (rich-console-93r)

`console.print({ a: 1 })` emitted a blank line. Every argument that was not
already a renderable went through `String()`, which for an object yields
`[object Object]` — text the markup parser then read as a style tag and
consumed whole, leaving nothing at all.

`print` now sorts each argument into three arms, and they are the whole domain:
a renderable draws itself; a string is the only kind of argument that can
contain markup, so it is the only kind the markup dialect is applied to;
everything else is data, formatted by `Pretty`. Running a markup parser over
`String(42)` only ever worked by accident, and that accident is gone.

`Pretty` had to become correct first. It rendered a `Date`, an `Error`, and a
`RegExp` as `{}`, because `Object.keys` on any of them is empty — so routing
objects to it would have traded one silent information loss for another. It now
asks whether a value carries its own string form: a `toString` other than
`Object.prototype`'s means the value answers the display question itself, and
inheriting the default means the keys are all the information there is. Both
clauses of that predicate are load-bearing — the second makes
`Object.create(null)`, which has no `toString` at all, reflect rather than throw.
`print` used to throw a TypeError on such a value.

`Pretty` moves from `renderables/` to `core/`. Reaching it from `console.ts`
would have been a third sanctioned upward edge out of `core/`, and CLAUDE.md
says in the imperative that a third edge is the signal to reconsider the seam
rather than append to the list. Reconsidered: `Pretty` composes no other
renderable — the trait every other file in `renderables/` shares — its imports
are core primitives only, and its job is `markup.ts`'s and `emoji.ts`'s job of
turning foreign input into `RichText`. Implementing `Renderable` was never the
criterion for that directory; `RichText` implements it too. The mis-cut was
`Pretty` living above core, so the edge is deleted rather than sanctioned.

One deliberate behavior change beyond the bug: a trailing options object is
recognised only when something precedes it. `print({ style: "..." })` now prints
the object instead of nothing, and no content is lost — options configure the
rendering of content, so a call with options and no content had nothing to
render either way.

The dead `item instanceof RichText` arm is deleted; `isRenderable` caught it
first, so it was unreachable.

Docs: `introduction.md` and `console.md` asserted this behavior and were false;
`pretty.md` had been corrected to the broken behavior and is now false in the
other direction. All three now match, against captured output. `console.md`'s
`log()` section loses the bare-timestamp case and keeps the `{ end: ... }` trap,
which is real.

fix(markup): settle what a legal plugin tag name is, once (rich-markup-pwr) (#89)

A registered plugin name matched as a bare PREFIX of the tag text, and the
failure was silent in both directions.

Registering `table` destroyed every `table.*` built-in: `[table.header]x[/table.header]`
fired the plugin and dropped the `.header` as attributes. The mirror case:
`register("a.b")` succeeded but `[a.b]` could never reach the handler, because
the tag scan stops at the dot.

Both ends wanted the same answer to "what is a legal plugin tag name?" and
neither asked it. There is now one source fragment, anchored two ways:

- MATCH: `^(name)(?=$|[ \t])` — a registered name addresses a plugin only when
  the tag text ends there or continues with the whitespace that introduces
  attributes. `[table.header]` and `[table=x]` fall through to the built-in
  dialect exactly as an unregistered name would.
- REGISTER: `^name$` — a name markup could never address is rejected loudly
  instead of installing an unreachable handler.

The two anchorings are mirrors: every name `register` accepts is one the match
site can reach, and every name it rejects is unreachable.

The six-line hand scanner it replaces is gone; `register` keeps its existing
reserved-name guard, which asked a different question (is this itself a valid
style?) and could not have caught either case.
